concepts.name: Wordpiece model (sub-word vocabulary)
concepts.summary: A data-driven sub-word vocabulary: words are split into a fixed set of common sub-word units, so any string can be encoded with no out-of-vocabulary tokens. The segmentation is deterministic and losslessly reversible.
concepts.explanation:
A wordpiece vocabulary is a fixed set of $D$ sub-word strings chosen from a training corpus.

Choosing them is a search. Given a target size $D$, the vocabulary is selected greedily to maximize the language-model likelihood of the training data under the evolving vocabulary. Equivalently, it seeks the $D$ pieces that segment the corpus into the fewest total tokens.

The search starts from a seed vocabulary of the basic characters. That seed is capped at a manageable number — roughly 500 for Western languages, more for Asian ones — with the remaining rare characters mapped to a single unknown-character symbol so they do not pollute the vocabulary.

Word boundaries have to survive the splitting. They are made recoverable by prepending a special marker character (written here as `_`) to the start of each word before training, and only at the start, not at both ends. Because every word begins with the marker and nothing else carries it, the original word sequence is reconstructed from the piece sequence without ambiguity.

An example makes the pattern visible. `Jet makers feud over seat width` segments as `_J et _makers _fe ud _over _seat _width`, where common words stay whole and rare ones split.

At inference the model emits a wordpiece sequence, which is then joined back into words as a post-processing step.

Vocabularies between 8k and 32k pieces are reported to give a good trade-off between accuracy and decoding speed.

For translation, a single shared vocabulary is trained over both source and target text. An identical string is then segmented identically on both sides, which makes copying names and numbers across languages easier to learn.

The scheme sits between two extremes. Character models are flexible but give long sequences and more compute; word models give short sequences but a closed vocabulary.

concepts.name: Length normalization penalty lp(Y)
concepts.summary: A divisor applied to a hypothesis's log-probability during beam search so that longer and shorter candidates can be compared fairly. It is controlled by a single exponent alpha.
concepts.explanation:
Beam search that ranks hypotheses by raw $\log P(Y\mid X)$ favors short outputs. Each decoding step adds another negative log-probability to the running total, so a longer sequence scores lower simply for being longer.

The fix is to divide the log-probability by a function of the length. Dividing by the length itself over-corrects. The refinement is to divide by $|Y|^{\alpha}$ with $0 < \alpha < 1$, which corrects only partly.

The form actually used is a shifted, normalized version of that:

$$lp(Y) = \frac{(5 + |Y|)^{\alpha}}{(5 + 1)^{\alpha}}$$

where $|Y|$ is the number of target tokens in the hypothesis.

Two constants, two jobs. The 5 added inside softens the penalty for very short hypotheses. Dividing by $(5+1)^{\alpha}$ makes $lp(Y)=1$ at length 1, so the scale of scores stays comparable across settings of $\alpha$.

The normalized score is $\log(P(Y\mid X))/lp(Y)$. Setting $\alpha = 0$ sends both powers to 1, giving $lp(Y)=1$, which recovers plain probability-ranked beam search.

Alpha is tuned on a development set. Values in $[0.6, 0.7]$ are reported as usually best when length normalization is used alone. A sweep run jointly with a [[coverage-penalty]] instead found a broad plateau of near-best scores, with the reported best at $\alpha = 0.2, \beta = 0.2$ (+1.1 BLEU over $\alpha=\beta=0$ on WMT'14 En→Fr dev).

The penalty affects ranking only. It does not change the model or the per-step distribution.

concepts.name: Coverage penalty cp(X; Y)
concepts.summary: An extra term in the beam-search score that rewards hypotheses whose attention has spread over the whole source sentence. It is controlled by a weight beta and is optional.
concepts.explanation:
The coverage penalty is added to the length-normalized score. Its purpose is to discourage under-translation, where the decoder ignores part of the input.

The notation comes first. Let $p_{i,j}$ be the attention probability the $j$-th target token places on the $i$-th source token, so that for each target step the attention weights sum to 1 over the source.

Total attention received by source token $i$ is then the column sum $\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} p_{i,j}$, and the penalty is assembled from those totals:

$$cp(X; Y) = \beta \sum_{i=1}^{|X|} \log\left(\min\left(\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} p_{i,j},\; 1.0\right)\right).$$

Two pieces of that expression carry the behavior. The $\min$ with 1.0 caps the credit each source token can earn, so attending to one token repeatedly does not help. The $\log$ makes source tokens that receive almost no attention very costly.

The complete ranking score puts both terms together:

$$s(Y, X) = \frac{\log(P(Y\mid X))}{lp(Y)} + cp(X; Y),$$

with $lp$ the length-normalization divisor. Setting $\alpha = 0$ and $\beta = 0$ reduces this to pure probability-based beam search.

Because the term reads the attention matrix, it applies only to architectures that expose one. And a decoder can use the length normalization without it, by setting $\beta = 0$.

The reported effect is smaller for models already fine-tuned with a sequence-level objective, since those learn to cover the source anyway.

concepts.name: Beam search pruning and early termination
concepts.summary: Beyond keeping a fixed number of hypotheses, the decoder prunes candidates that fall a fixed margin below the current best, both per-step and among finished hypotheses. This is what makes search stop early instead of running to a fixed maximum length.
concepts.explanation:
The decoder keeps a beam of typically 8-12 hypotheses, with 4 or 2 reported to cost only slightly in quality.

On top of that fixed beam width, two threshold prunes are applied. Both use a margin in log-score units, typically $3.0$. That margin is confusingly also called `beamsize`, and it is a different quantity from the number of hypotheses.

The first prune runs per step. Only tokens whose local score is within the margin of the best token at that step are expanded.

The second runs across finished hypotheses. Once a normalized best score exists under the ranking function, any hypothesis more than the margin below that best normalized score is dropped. This prune applies only to complete hypotheses, because the normalized score involves the length penalty and is well defined only when a hypothesis ends.

Its practical effect is early termination. As soon as one sufficiently good complete hypothesis exists, nearly all remaining partial hypotheses fall out of the beam and search stops, rather than continuing to a fixed cap.

Without this pruning the fallback is to decode to a predetermined maximum output length, set to twice the source length. The pruning is reported to speed up CPU search by 30-40% versus that fallback.

Batching complicates termination slightly. When many sentences are decoded in parallel — typically up to 35, batched by similar length — the batch finishes only when every sentence's hypotheses are out of beam, which the paper reports costs little in practice.
